prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B019 is the only candidate on which all six of us placed first, but I do not rest the case on that agreement. The discovery meets the standard I would apply to any field: a specific, identifiable change in how a field understands a process, followed by confirmation over decades. Incretin physiology, proglucagon processing, the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide and its actions on islets, gut and appetite established a new endocrine axis, and the basic science was then validated by approved drugs and large randomized outcome trials. The arc from hormone biology to patient benefit is unusually well documented, independently replicated and still widening. A prize credited to the hormone discovery (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov) stays within the three-person limit and honours the physiological discovery on which the drugs rest, rather than a single product.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution, not merit. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested against groups not in the credited list (Habener is repeatedly mentioned by colleagues, and I cannot verify the history from the supplied text), and excluding Knudsen sets a precedent that the industrial design of long-acting analogues (liraglutide, semaglutide), which is what actually reached patients at scale, is not recognised. If the committee decides that the prize should reward the medicine as much as the physiology, my trio is the wrong one. There is also a risk that unanimity at the opening stage hides how different our unstated views are on basic discovery versus drug development.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B019 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov but flags that the committee must decide whether to honour drug development (Knudsen) over one of the physiology contributors. He also ranks B012 second and treats the six-name optogenetics allocation as a genuine problem.
responses.response: I agree that the Knudsen question is the real open point for B019 and I do not think it is resolved by calling her work industrial. The semaglutide chemistry is a scientific advance in its own right. My reason for keeping her out is narrower: with a three-person cap, the discovery of the hormone's action is the part that changed the field's understanding, and Holst and Drucker's physiology is what made the drug target credible. I would revisit if the committee wants the citation to cover the drug. On B012 I am less moved than he is: I placed it sixth because a six-person claim compressed into three leaves Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenboeck out, and a tool whose health impact is still early weighs less for me than for him. High originality is not enough on its own.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, ranks B019 first and B012 second, and notes that the optogenetics case is a methodological revolution with early clinical translation, with six credited names exceeding the three-laureate limit. He places the UPR (B040) fourth as a compact two-person case.
responses.response: We agree on the allocation problem in B012 and I take his point that the tool has transformed circuit analysis, which is a real change in the field. Where I differ is on what that does for a medicine prize: the clinical translation is still a few retinal cases. I would put B040 higher than he does. Walter and Mori are a clean pair, the UPR is mechanistically complete and confirmed over three decades, and its relevance to diabetes, neurodegeneration and secretory-cell disease is growing. The fact that its medical impact is mostly mechanistic rather than a single drug is a weakness only if one reads the prize narrowly, and the rules do not require that.

responses.point: El Manira ranks B012 second, argues it transformed causal circuit neuroscience including motor circuits, and ranks the cGAS-STING pathway (B024) fourth while placing B030 CAR-T third.
responses.response: I respect the neuroscience argument, but I think the strongest version of it is also the strongest case against: the impact is on how experiments are done, with the medical benefit still prospective. I would also push back gently on B024. Chen's cGAS and cGAMP discovery is excellent and probably deserving in time, but the credit list includes three junior co-authors and omits Vance and others, so allocation within two or three names would be harder than for B040 or B030, and I would not move it above them yet. On CAR-T we agree it is an important candidate, and I share his worry that Eshhar is outside the credited names.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B019, B012 and B040 as his top three and prefers Hall and Schreiber for TOR (B027), ranking CAR-T (B030) only fifth.
responses.response: I agree that B040 belongs with B019 near the top and that Mori and Walter are a coherent two-person prize. I would differ on CAR-T: I think it ranks above where he places it, because the clinical effect in refractory B-cell malignancies is unambiguous and independently replicated, and it created a new class of living drug. On TOR I am more cautious about including Schreiber, whose rapamycin and FKBP work is chemical context to the discovery of the target in yeast; I put Hall alone as the clearer attribution, though I also see why he thinks two names is cleaner.

uncertainties: Whether the active GLP-1 peptide priority dispute (Mojsov versus Habener and others) is as serious as colleagues suggest, since it cannot be settled from the supplied text.
Whether the committee will credit drug design (Knudsen) alongside, or instead of, one of the physiology contributors.
Whether the prize should be one achievement or two; a second part, such as B040 or B030, would force us to cut B019 to fewer names.
Whether the CAR-T attribution without Eshhar would be defensible.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I co-authored nuclear-receptor work with Ronald Evans and have collaborated with Per Svenningsson and Johan Ericson, but none of these people is credited on a shortlisted ballot, so I see no reason to recuse.
